docs.title: fetch_contents()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (nested inside crawl_github_files) Signature: def fetch_contents(path: str) -> None:

Description: The primary recursive directory traversal and file fetching engine for the GitHub REST API implementation.

    def fetch_contents(path):
        """Fetch contents of the repository at a specific path and commit"""
        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}"
        params = {"ref": ref} if ref is not None else {}

        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and "rate limit exceeded" in response.text.lower():
            if not token:
                raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")
            reset_time = int(response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset", 0))
            wait_time = max(reset_time - time.time(), 0) + 1
            emit_raw("WARNING", f"Rate limit exceeded. Waiting for {wait_time:.0f} seconds...")
            time.sleep(wait_time)
            return fetch_contents(path)

        if response.status_code == 404:
            if not token:
                emit_raw(
                    "ERROR",
                    "Error 404: Repository not found or is private.\n"
                    "If this is a private repository, please provide a valid GitHub token via the 'token' argument or set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable.",
                )
            elif not path and ref == "main":
                emit_raw(
                    "ERROR",
                    "Error 404: Repository not found. Check if the default branch is not 'main'\n"
                    "Try adding branch name to the request i.e. python main.py --repo https://github.com/username/repo/tree/master",
                )
            else:
                emit_raw(
                    "ERROR",
                    f"Error 404: Path '{path}' not found in repository or insufficient permissions with the provided token.\n"
                    f"Please verify the token has access to this repository and the path exists.",
                )
            return None

        if response.status_code != 200:
            emit_raw("ERROR", f"Error fetching {path}: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
            return None

        contents = response.json()

        # Handle both single file and directory responses
        if not isinstance(contents, list):
            contents = [contents]
// ... loop through contents items: file downloading / base64 decode and recursive dir calls ...

fetch_contents queries /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}. It handles rate limits by checking response status codes and body text for throttling indicators. If throttled with a valid token, it extracts X-RateLimit-Reset, sleeps until the reset time passes, and retries the request.

For directory entries, it checks exclusion patterns and recurses. For files, it retrieves raw content via download_url or base64 decoding, enforces max_file_size, and stores decoded text in the enclosing files dictionary.

Parameters: * path (str): Repository-relative path to a directory or file.

Returns: * None: Mutates the shared files dictionary and api_counters mapping in the enclosing scope.

Raises: * Exception: Raised when GitHub API rate limits are encountered without an authentication token.

docs.title: Crawl Result Dictionary
docs.text:
The return payload produced by crawl_github_files follows a two-key dictionary schema:

Field Type Description files dict[str, str] Key-value store mapping normalized repository file paths to UTF-8 file contents. stats dict[str, Any] Detailed telemetry and filter metadata tracking operation results.

docs.title: stats Sub-Dictionary Schema
docs.text: Field Type Description Example downloaded_count int Total number of files successfully read and stored. 42 skipped_count int Total files bypassed (used in local crawl parity; initialized to 0). 0 skipped_files list[str] List of paths skipped during ingestion. [] base_path str \| None Root sub-path trimmed when use_relative_paths is enabled. "src/core" include_patterns set[str] \| None Set of glob inclusion rules applied during traversal. {"*.py", "*.md"} exclude_patterns set[str] \| None Set of glob exclusion rules applied during traversal. {"tests/*"} source str (Optional) Present only during SSH clones; set to "ssh_clone". "ssh_clone" error str (Optional) Error description present only if an SSH clone failure occurs. "Repository not found"

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: The module implements multi-tiered error handling to address network, authentication, and file decoding issues across both crawling engines:

docs.title: API Rate Limit Throttling
docs.text: GitHub limits unauthenticated API requests to 60 per hour, while authenticated requests receive 5,000 per hour. When the API returns an HTTP 403 or 429 status code indicating rate limits: * Unauthenticated Requests: Execution halts immediately with an Exception instructing the user to configure a GITHUB_TOKEN. * Authenticated Requests: The module extracts the X-RateLimit-Reset Unix epoch timestamp, calculates the sleep duration (reset_time - time.time() + 1), logs a warning, and blocks via time.sleep before retrying the failed request.

docs.title: HTTP 404 Disambiguation
docs.text: The module provides contextual diagnostics for HTTP 404 responses: 1. Unauthenticated 404: Recommends supplying a GITHUB_TOKEN in case the target repository is private. 2. Authenticated 404 on Root (ref == "main"): Warns that the default branch may be master rather than main, advising explicit branch declaration. 3. Subpath 404: Distinguishes between nonexistent file paths and insufficient token permissions.

docs.title: Binary and Non-UTF-8 Rejection
docs.text: The crawler exclusively ingests text-based source code: * In the SSH engine, files are decoded using the utf-8-sig codec. Catches for UnicodeDecodeError and ValueError increment count_non_text and append the path to skipped_non_text_list without halting directory traversal. * In the REST API engine, payload sizes are validated against max_file_size prior to base64 decoding (using a len(content) * 0.75 size heuristic). Any decoding failure logs CRAWL_FILE_HTTP_ERROR or CRAWL_FILE_UNEXPECTED and skips the entry.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
Following the remote repository extraction capabilities established in crawl_github_files.py, the utils/crawl_local_files.py module serves as the primary ingestion gateway for local directory trees within the documentation pipeline. It implements an in-place filesystem crawler that traverses directories, evaluates hierarchical ignore patterns, enforces safety limits on file sizes and encoding formats, and delivers a normalized dictionary of file paths mapped to their string contents. This output provides the raw text corpus consumed by downstream tokenization, chunking, and LLM processing stages.

The module solves several operational challenges inherent to processing arbitrary local codebases: handling deeply nested .gitignore files relative to their declaring directories, preventing unbounded memory consumption when encountering binary or oversized build artifacts, and pruning directory branches early during traversal to avoid unnecessary filesystem overhead. To achieve parity with the GitHub crawler, crawl_local_files.py supports standard fnmatch inclusion and exclusion globs alongside formal Git wildcard path specifications powered by the pathspec library.

The architectural flow is structured as an integrated single-pass traversal over the filesystem using os.walk. As the crawler descends into the tree, it dynamically registers nested .gitignore specifications, prunes subdirectories in-place before they can be traversed, filters candidate files against pattern cascades, validates byte size thresholds, and decodes content with UTF-8 byte order mark (utf-8-sig) handling. Telemetry events and real-time operational metrics are emitted throughout execution using utils/output.py.

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_local_files(directory: str, include_patterns: set | None = None, exclude_patterns: set | None = None, max_file_size: int | None = None, use_relative_paths: bool = True) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]:

Description: Crawls a local directory tree in a single pass using os.walk, dynamically compiling nested .gitignore configurations, applying directory and file pattern matching, rejecting binary or oversized assets, and aggregating file contents into a unified dictionary structure.

Parameters: * directory (str): System path pointing to the root directory to crawl. * include_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns (e.g., {"*.py", "*.ts"}) defining files that must be included. If provided, files not matching at least one pattern are omitted. * exclude_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns (e.g., {"tests/*", "*.lock"}) matching files or directories that must be skipped. * max_file_size (int | None): Maximum allowable file size in bytes. Files exceeding this threshold are bypassed. * use_relative_paths (bool): When True, returns dictionary keys formatted relative to directory. When False, returns absolute filesystem paths. Defaults to True.

Returns: * dict: A dictionary containing a single key "files", mapping string file paths to their decoded text contents: {"files": {filepath: content}}.

Raises: * ValueError: If directory does not exist or is not a valid filesystem directory.

docs.title: Phase 1: Validation and State Initialization
docs.text:
if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []

    # --- Gitignore specs: {abs_dir_path: pathspec} ---
    gitignore_specs = {}
    root_gi_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    if os.path.exists(root_gi_path):
        spec = _load_gitignore(root_gi_path)
        if spec:
            gitignore_specs[os.path.abspath(directory)] = spec
            emit("CRAWL_GITIGNORE_LOADED", path=root_gi_path)

    # Translated reason strings (looked up once)
    reason_excluded = get("CRAWL_REASON_EXCLUDED")
    reason_gitignore = get("CRAWL_REASON_GITIGNORE")

The function initiates by verifying that the supplied path exists and represents a valid directory via os.path.isdir, raising an immediate ValueError if the assertion fails. It establishes the central extraction dictionary files_dict alongside metrics counters tracking candidate entry indices, successfully ingested files, pattern exclusions, size violations, and non-text decodings.

Before starting the directory walk, it detects whether a .gitignore exists at the root of the specified directory. If present, it compiles the rules into a pathspec.PathSpec object using _load_gitignore() and maps it to the absolute path of the target directory. Localized reason strings (reason_excluded and reason_gitignore) are retrieved once from utils.output.get to avoid redundant dictionary lookups throughout the traversal loop.

docs.title: Phase 2: Directory Walk and Nested Ignore Discovery
docs.text:
# --- Single-pass: walk, filter, and process inline ---
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        abs_root = os.path.abspath(root)

        # Check for nested .gitignore in current directory (skip root, already loaded)
        if abs_root != os.path.abspath(directory):
            nested_gi = os.path.join(root, ".gitignore")
            if os.path.exists(nested_gi):
                spec = _load_gitignore(nested_gi)
                if spec:
                    gitignore_specs[abs_root] = spec

The traversal operates via Python's standard os.walk, inspecting the directory hierarchy top-down. For every directory entered, the crawler resolves the absolute root path abs_root to eliminate symlink and relative reference ambiguity.

If the current directory is not the crawl root, the routine checks for a nested .gitignore file. If located, _load_gitignore() parses its patterns and records the resulting PathSpec into the gitignore_specs registry under abs_root. This scoping design ensures that ignore rules declared in subpackages or nested modules are discovered dynamically before processing the subdirectories or files enclosed beneath them.

docs.title: Phase 3: Directory Filtering and In-Place Branch Pruning
docs.text:
# --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            abs_d = os.path.join(abs_root, d)
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(abs_d, directory)

            reason = None
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_d, is_dir=True):
                reason = reason_gitignore
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern.removesuffix("/*")
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = reason_excluded
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_DIR_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=dirpath_rel, reason=reason)

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()

Directory filtering enforces branch pruning directly within os.walk by mutating the dirs list in place. Subdirectories are sorted deterministically before evaluation. For each subdirectory d, the crawler checks if its absolute path matches any active rule in gitignore_specs via _matches_any_gitignore(..., is_dir=True).

If not ignored by Git rules, the directory is checked against exclude_patterns. To account for user patterns containing trailing wildcard syntax like tests/* or node_modules/*, the loop strips the trailing /* suffix and evaluates both the relative path (dirpath_rel) and directory name (d) using fnmatch.fnmatch. Matching directories are registered in excluded_dirs, incrementing exclusion metrics and broadcasting a CRAWL_DIR_EXCLUDED event. Modifying dirs with dirs.remove(d) prevents os.walk from descending into the excluded subtrees entirely, significantly reducing unnecessary filesystem I/O. The surviving directories are re-sorted to preserve consistent cross-platform traversal ordering.

docs.title: Phase 4: File Exclusion and Inclusion Matching
docs.text:
# --- File processing (inline, sorted) ---
        for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            abs_filepath = os.path.abspath(filepath)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore (all levels)
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_filepath):
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_INCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                    continue

For every file in the surviving directory, the filename is sorted and resolved to its relative path or absolute path based on use_relative_paths. The candidate is subjected to a three-tier rejection filter: 1. Gitignore Evaluation: Evaluated against all applicable gitignore_specs using _matches_any_gitignore(). Matches trigger a CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE event and skip the file. 2. Exclusion Globs: Evaluated against the caller's exclude_patterns using fnmatch.fnmatch. Matches trigger a CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED event and skip the file. 3. Inclusion Globs: If include_patterns is defined, the file path must match at least one glob pattern. Failure to match triggers a CRAWL_FILE_NOT_INCLUDED event and skips the file.

All skips increment the count_excluded metric and advance the global entry tracking counter entry_num.

docs.title: Phase 5: Size Enforcement and Text Ingestion
docs.text:
# Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_SIZE_LIMIT", num=entry_num, path=relpath, size=f"{size_kb:.0f}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_ERROR", num=entry_num, path=relpath, error=e)

Files passing the pattern filters are verified against max_file_size using os.path.getsize. If the byte size exceeds the configured ceiling, the crawler records the path in skipped_size_limit, increments count_size_limit, emits CRAWL_FILE_SIZE_LIMIT with the calculated size in kilobytes, and bypasses content extraction.

If the size falls within acceptable limits, the module attempts to open and read the file using utf-8-sig encoding, ensuring automatic stripping of UTF-8 byte order marks. If decoding succeeds, the string content is placed into files_dict keyed by relpath, count_processed is incremented, and CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED is emitted. If a UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError occurs (typical for binary assets, images, or compiled objects), the exception is trapped, the file is added to skipped_non_text, and CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT is dispatched. Generic I/O or filesystem permission errors are caught by the broader Exception block, emitting CRAWL_FILE_ERROR without terminating the crawl.

docs.title: Phase 6: Telemetry Reporting and Result Packaging
docs.text:
# --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_HEADER")
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_TOTAL", count=total_fetched)
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_PROCESSED", count=count_processed)
    if count_excluded > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_EXCLUDED", count=count_excluded)
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_SIZE_LIMIT", count=count_size_limit)
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)
    if count_non_text > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_NON_TEXT", count=count_non_text)
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)

    return {"files": files_dict}

Following the complete traversal of directory, the crawler calculates total inspected items by summing processed, excluded, size-limited, and non-text counts. It emits a structured sequence of telemetry summary events (CRAWL_SUMMARY_HEADER, CRAWL_SUMMARY_TOTAL, CRAWL_SUMMARY_PROCESSED, and conditional breakdown items for size-limited or non-text files). Finally, it packages and returns files_dict encapsulated under the "files" key, conforming to the unified schema expected across all ingestion handlers in the codebase.

Usage Example: The standalone execution block in crawl_local_files.py demonstrates the public usage pattern of invoking the function with exclusion filters on a relative parent path:

from utils.crawl_local_files import crawl_local_files
from utils.output import emit_raw

emit_raw("INFO", "--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
files_data = crawl_local_files(
    "..",
    exclude_patterns={
        "*.pyc",
        "__pycache__/*",
        ".venv/*",
        ".git/*",
        "docs/*",
        "output/*",
    },
)
emit_raw("INFO", f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
for path in files_data["files"]:
    emit_raw("INFO", f"  {path}")

docs.title: _load_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Internal (Module-private) Signature: def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path: str) -> pathspec.PathSpec | None:

Description: Opens and parses a .gitignore file from the local filesystem, returning a compiled pathspec.PathSpec object configured with the gitwildmatch pattern syntax. If the file cannot be accessed or parsed due to I/O or syntax faults, it intercepts the exception, logs a warning message to the execution log, and returns None to prevent traversal failure.

Parameters: * gitignore_path (str): Absolute or relative filesystem path to the target .gitignore file.

Returns: * pathspec.PathSpec | None: A compiled PathSpec matcher representing the gitignore rules, or None if loading failed.

Raises: * No exceptions are propagated; all file access and parsing errors are intercepted internally.

Implementation: 

def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path):
    """Load a .gitignore file and return a PathSpec, or None on failure."""
    try:
        with open(gitignore_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            return pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", f.readlines())
    except Exception as e:
        emit_raw("WARNING", f"Failed to load .gitignore at {gitignore_path}: {e}", dest="LOG")
        return None

The function utilizes open with utf-8-sig encoding to handle ignore files that may contain Unicode characters or byte order markers. The lines read from the file are passed directly to pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines using the standard gitwildmatch pattern parser, which faithfully replicates Git's native wildcard matching rules (including prefix slashes, directory trailing slashes, and negation with !). If any error occurs—such as a FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, or file locking conflict—it catches Exception, logs the error using emit_raw(..., dest="LOG"), and safely yields None.

Example: 

root_gi_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
if os.path.exists(root_gi_path):
    spec = _load_gitignore(root_gi_path)
    if spec:
        gitignore_specs[os.path.abspath(directory)] = spec
        emit("CRAWL_GITIGNORE_LOADED", path=root_gi_path)

docs.title: _matches_any_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Internal (Module-private) Signature: def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs: dict[str, pathspec.PathSpec], abs_path: str, is_dir: bool = False) -> bool:

Description: Evaluates whether an absolute filesystem path matches any loaded .gitignore specification within the active hierarchy. The function calculates the path relative to each ignore specification's parent directory, ensures Windows backslashes are normalized to POSIX forward slashes, appends trailing slashes for directory matching, and checks for rule inclusion.

Parameters: * gitignore_specs (dict[str, pathspec.PathSpec]): Dictionary mapping absolute directory paths to their corresponding compiled PathSpec objects. * abs_path (str): Absolute filesystem path of the candidate file or directory being evaluated. * is_dir (bool): Boolean flag indicating whether abs_path represents a directory (True) or a file (False). Defaults to False.

Returns: * bool: True if the path matches at least one applicable .gitignore rule; False otherwise.

Raises: * No exceptions are raised.

Implementation: 

def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_path, is_dir=False):
    """Check if a path matches ANY loaded .gitignore spec.

    Each spec is checked with the path relative to its own .gitignore directory.
    For directories, a trailing '/' is appended for proper gitignore matching.

    Args:
        gitignore_specs: dict of {abs_dir_path: pathspec.PathSpec}
        abs_path: absolute path of the file or directory to check
        is_dir: True if checking a directory
    Returns:
        True if the path matches any gitignore rule
    """
    for gi_dir, spec in gitignore_specs.items():
        rel = os.path.relpath(abs_path, gi_dir)
        # Skip if the path is not under this gitignore's scope
        if rel.startswith(".."):
            continue
        match_path = rel.replace("\\", "/")
        if is_dir:
            match_path = match_path.rstrip("/") + "/"
        if spec.match_file(match_path):
            return True
    return False

The function iterates through every registered (gi_dir, spec) pair. It computes the relative path from the .gitignore declaring directory (gi_dir) to the target candidate (abs_path) using os.path.relpath. If the resulting path begins with .., the target lies outside the scope of that specific .gitignore and evaluation for that spec is skipped.

For targets falling within the scope, platform-specific path separators (\) are normalized to standard Unix slashes (/). If is_dir is True, any trailing slashes are stripped and a single trailing / is appended, which enables pathspec to correctly trigger directory-only ignore patterns (such as build/ or dist/). If spec.match_file(match_path) evaluates to True, the function immediately halts iteration and returns True. If no matching rules are found across all scopes, it returns False.

Example: 

# Matching directories during traversal:
if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_d, is_dir=True):
    reason = reason_gitignore

# Matching candidate files during processing:
if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_filepath):
    count_excluded += 1
    emit("CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
    continue

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The module incorporates multi-layered defensive exception handling to guarantee that non-standard files, encoding anomalies, or permission errors do not terminate execution mid-crawl:

  1. Target Directory Validation:

  2. Prior to entering os.walk, os.path.isdir(directory) checks if the root path is accessible. An invalid or non-existent path immediately raises a descriptive ValueError.

  3. Gitignore Parsing Resilience:

  4. In _load_gitignore(), file opening and parsing operations are enclosed in a generic try...except Exception block. If a .gitignore file is locked, unreadable, or contains invalid syntax, an alert is dispatched via emit_raw("WARNING", ..., dest="LOG") and the function returns None. The crawl continues uninterrupted without the failed specification.

  5. Binary and Non-Text Asset Interception:

  6. When reading file content via open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig"), binary files (executables, compiled bytecode, images) or files with incompatible encodings trigger UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError. The crawler traps these exceptions, classifies the file as non-text, updates count_non_text, records the path in skipped_non_text, and emits CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT.

  7. I/O and Permission Fault Containment:

  8. Any unexpected filesystem errors occurring during file access (such as PermissionError on restricted files or transient OS read locks) are intercepted by a catch-all except Exception as e clause. The crawler logs CRAWL_FILE_ERROR with the associated exception object, increments count_non_text, and proceeds to the next candidate file.

docs.title: exclude_patterns.py
docs.text: Source: utils/exclude_patterns.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/exclude_patterns.py serves as the centralized pattern registry and exclusion filter baseline for all ingestion mechanisms across the codebase documentation pipeline. Following the directory traversal and file-system extraction capabilities established in crawl_local_files.py, this module externalizes file and directory skip rules, decoupling discovery logic from crawling policies. By consolidating common build outputs, virtual environments, version control metadata, multimedia binaries, package dependencies, and vendor artifacts into a unified data structure, it ensures that only human-authored, documentation-relevant source files reach downstream AST parsing, token counting, and LLM summarization.

The module exports a static configuration set, DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS, formatted according to Unix glob syntax compatible with the standard library fnmatch module. Directory exclusions explicitly use trailing wildcards (for example, dist/*, node_modules/*, .git/*) to enable in-place subtree pruning during directory walking algorithms (os.walk), while individual file exclusions target binary, compressed, lockfile, and generated formats using extension patterns (such as *.png, *.zip, *.lock) or fixed basenames (such as .DS_Store, Thumbs.db, package-lock.json). In addition to traditional software engineering artifacts, the registry features comprehensive exclusions for modern AI agent configuration directories and scratchpads (such as .cursor/*, .windsurf/*, .cline/*, .roo/*, and .copilot/*), preventing transient tool states and model prompt dumps from leaking into synthesized repository architectures.

docs.title: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS: set[str]

Description: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS is a module-level constant containing an unmodifiable-by-convention set of glob pattern strings. It defines standard ignore rules for repository scanning across both local and remote filesystems. The patterns are organized into seven logical categories covering binary assets, build targets, dependency directories, language-specific compiled artifacts, OS metadata, IDE configurations, and AI agent workdirs. Each pattern follows standard fnmatch glob syntax. Trailing slashes followed by asterisks (/*) denote directory trees that should be skipped entirely, allowing crawler engines to prune traversal branches before descending into subdirectories.

docs.title: Category 1: Media, Data, and Static Assets
docs.text:
DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS = {
    # 1. Media, Data, and Static Assets
    "assets/*",
    "data/*",
    "images/*",
    "public/*",
    "static/*",
    "temp/*",
    "tmp/*",
    "media/*",
    "*.jpg",
    "*.jpeg",
    "*.png",
    "*.gif",
    "*.ico",
    "*.svg",
    "*.webp",
    "*.mp4",
    "*.webm",
    "*.mov",
    "*.mp3",
    "*.wav",
    "*.pdf",
    "*.doc",
    "*.docx",
    "*.xls",
    "*.xlsx",
    "*.ppt",
    "*.pptx",
    "*.zip",
    "*.tar",
    "*.gz",
    "*.rar",
    "*.7z",
    # ...

This section filters out high-overhead binary assets, pre-rendered media, temporary runtime scratchpads, and office documents that cannot be interpreted as source code or AST components. File extensions such as .jpg, .png, .webp, .mp4, and .wav represent raw multimedia files that would otherwise cause UnicodeDecodeError exceptions or waste LLM context budgets if ingested as raw bytes. Archive formats (*.zip, *.tar, *.gz, *.rar, *.7z) and office suite formats (*.docx, *.xlsx, *.pptx, *.pdf) are similarly omitted because their compressed and proprietary binary encodings cannot be processed by text summarization models without specialized document-parsing pipelines.

docs.title: Category 2: Build, Distribution, and Framework Caches
docs.text:
# ...
    # 2. Build, Distribution, and Framework Caches
    "dist/*",
    "build/*",
    "out/*",
    "output/*",
    "output-test*/*",
    "target/*",
    "bin/*",
    "obj/*",
    ".next/*",
    ".nuxt/*",
    ".svelte-kit/*",
    ".expo/*",
    "docs/*",
    "test/*",
    "tests/*",
    "examples/*",
    "v1/*",
    "experimental/*",
    "deprecated/*",
    "misc/*",
    "legacy/*",
    "*.log",
    "*.bak",
    "*.tmp",
    "*.swp",
    # ...

This section targets transient build outputs, bundled web framework runtimes, test suites, and auxiliary repository directories. Framework-specific compilation caches such as Next.js (.next/*), Nuxt (.nuxt/*), SvelteKit (.svelte-kit/*), and Expo (.expo/*) contain heavily bundled, minified JavaScript and source maps that distort codebase understanding and exhaust token budgets. Directory patterns for dist/*, build/*, target/*, bin/*, and obj/* prevent compiled intermediate representation files from polluting the symbol index. Additionally, test suites (test/*, tests/*), documentation (docs/*), and auxiliary development folders (examples/*, legacy/*, deprecated/*) are skipped to keep the generated documentation strictly focused on active, production-grade source architecture.

docs.title: Category 3: Environments, Dependencies, and Lockfiles
docs.text:
# ...
    # 3. Environments, Dependencies & Lockfiles
    "venv/*",
    ".venv/*",
    "env/*",
    ".env",
    ".env.*",
    "node_modules/*",
    "bower_components/*",
    "jspm_packages/*",
    "vendor/*",
    "packages/*",
    "*.lock",
    "package-lock.json",
    "yarn.lock",
    "pnpm-lock.yaml",
    "Cargo.lock",
    "Gemfile.lock",
    "poetry.lock",
    "mix.lock",
    "Pipfile.lock",

This segment prevents crawlers from scanning external dependencies and configuration secrets. Virtual environments (venv/*, .venv/*, env/*) and third-party dependency trees (node_modules/*, vendor/*, packages/*) represent external library code rather than the repository's native implementation logic; scanning them would cause massive memory allocation spikes and introduce millions of irrelevant tokens. Environment files (.env, .env.*) are excluded to avoid accidentally leaking API keys, database credentials, or secret tokens into prompts dispatched to remote LLM providers. Lockfiles (*.lock, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, Cargo.lock, poetry.lock) are also excluded because their massive dependency graphs contain high-frequency hash listings that degrade prompt context quality.

docs.text:
# ...

    "__pycache__/*",
    "*.pyc",

    "*.pyd",
    ".pytest_cache/*",

    ".gradle/*",

    "*.o",

    "ios/Pods/*",
    "android/.gradle/*",
    "android/app/build/*",  # Mobile
    # ...

This segment isolates runtime-compiled bytecode, testing tool caches, and native platform binaries across Python, Java/JVM, C/C++, and mobile environments. For Python projects, it intercepts bytecode caches (__pycache__/*, *.pyc, *.pyo, *.pyd) and analysis metadata (.pytest_cache/*, .ruff_cache/*, .tox/*, .coverage, htmlcov/*). For Java and JVM runtimes, it eliminates compiler caches (.gradle/*) and compiled Java packages (*.class, *.jar, *.war). For native ecosystems (C, C++, Rust, Go), it blocks compiled object files and libraries (*.o, *.obj, *.so, *.dylib, *.dll, *.lib, *.a, *.exe). For mobile stacks, CocoaPods installations (ios/Pods/*) and Gradle Android build artifacts (android/.gradle/*, android/app/build/*) are skipped directly at the root level.

docs.title: Category 5: OS and Version Control Metadata
docs.text:
# ...
    # 5. OS & Version Control
    ".git/*",
    ".github/*",
    ".svn/*",
    ".hg/*",
    ".DS_Store",
    "Thumbs.db",
    "desktop.ini",
    # ...

This section blocks version control internals and operating system desktop metadata. VCS trees such as Git internals (.git/*), SVN repositories (.svn/*), and Mercurial trees (.hg/*) contain object databases, index packfiles, and internal hooks that do not represent application source code. While .github/* contains CI/CD workflow YAML definitions, it is filtered out from source architecture synthesis to keep the generated documentation strictly oriented around application source mechanics. OS-generated desktop database files (.DS_Store on macOS, Thumbs.db and desktop.ini on Windows) are excluded to prevent cross-platform file conflicts and non-text reading errors during crawling.

docs.title: Category 6: Classic IDE Configuration Files
docs.text:
# ...
    # 6. Classic IDEs
    ".vscode/*",
    ".idea/*",
    "*.iml",
    ".eclipse/*",
    ".settings/*",
    ".classpath",
    ".project",
    ".vs/*",
    # ...

This group targets developer environment metadata generated by traditional Integrated Development Environments (IDEs). Directories and files from Visual Studio Code (.vscode/*), JetBrains IntelliJ / PyCharm (.idea/*, *.iml), Eclipse (.eclipse/*, .settings/*, .classpath, .project), and Visual Studio (.vs/*) represent user-specific workspace configurations, local launch targets, editor preferences, and cached project models. Excluding these prevents developer-specific settings from altering repository architectures or cluttering pipeline context.

docs.title: Category 7: AI Agents and Modern AI IDE Metadata
docs.text:
# ...
    # 7. AI Agents & Modern AI IDEs
    ".cursor/*",
    ".cursorrules",
    ".windsurf/*",
    ".windsurfrules",
    ".cline/*",
    ".clinerules",
    ".roo/*",
    ".roorules",
    ".agent/*",
    ".agents/*",
    ".continue/*",
    ".aide/*",
    ".gemini/*",
    ".antigravity/*",
    ".claude/*",
    ".copilot/*",
}

This section excludes configuration directories, operational logs, instructions, and scratchpad storage generated by modern AI development environments and autonomous code generation agents. Toolchains such as Cursor (.cursor/*, .cursorrules), Windsurf (.windsurf/*, .windsurfrules), Cline (.cline/*, .clinerules), Roo Code (.roo/*, .roorules), Continue (.continue/*), GitHub Copilot (.copilot/*), Claude Code (.claude/*), and related AI agents (.agent/*, .agents/*, .gemini/*, .antigravity/*, .aide/*) often write execution traces, prompt scratchpads, and context dumps directly to the repository tree. If crawled, these agent logs could create feedback loops in downstream LLM prompts or expose private agent orchestration steps in the final architecture documents.

Example Usage: 

# Extracted from crawler implementation in utils/crawl_local_files.py
from utils.exclude_patterns import DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS
import fnmatch
import os

# Evaluating directory branch pruning in os.walk
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(root_dir):
    # In-place mutation of dirs list stops os.walk from descending
    dirs[:] = [
        d for d in dirs
        if not any(
            fnmatch.fnmatch(d, pat.rstrip("/*")) or fnmatch.fnmatch(f"{d}/", pat)
            for pat in DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS
        )
    ]

docs.title: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS Registry Schema
docs.text:
DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS is instantiated as a Python set of strings. The data structure does not implement custom methods or subclasses; it serves as a configuration set. The table below details its structural contract and operational pattern groups:

Pattern Category Target Scope Syntax Convention Example Patterns Pipeline Impact 1. Media and Static Assets Binary files, static images, archives, docs prefix/*, *.ext images/*, *.png, *.zip, *.pdf Prevents UTF-8 decoding crashes and skips binary token waste. 2. Build and Caches Transformed outputs, build directories dirname/*, *.log dist/*, build/*, .next/*, *.log Skips minified artifacts, sourcemaps, logs, and compiled code. 3. Environments and Lockfiles Dependencies, secrets, lockfiles dirname/*, basename node_modules/*, .venv/*, .env, *.lock Eliminates external libraries and guards against secret leakage. 4. Language-Specific Compiled bytecode, runtime caches dirname/*, *.ext __pycache__/*, *.class, *.so, *.dll Prevents ingestion of machine-specific binary formats. 5. OS and VCS Version control, OS desktop databases dirname/*, basename .git/*, .DS_Store, Thumbs.db Stops crawlers from traversing VCS object graphs and OS cache files. 6. Classic IDEs Workspace configuration directories dirname/*, *.ext .vscode/*, .idea/*, *.iml, .vs/* Prevents local developer IDE state from influencing repo docs. 7. AI Agents and IDEs Agent scratchpads, rules, state dirs dirname/*, basename .cursor/*, .windsurf/*, .claude/* Avoids recursive agent ingestion loops and prompt transcript leakage.

docs.title: Structural Pattern Conventions
docs.text:
The patterns defined in DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS rely on two distinct syntactic conventions evaluated via Python's fnmatch module:

  1. Directory Branch Pruning Patterns (<directory_name>/*):
  2. Any pattern terminating with /* indicates an entire directory hierarchy.
  3. When processing local directories via os.walk, consuming modules strip the trailing /* via .rstrip("/*") or match against d + "/" to prune subdirectories in-place (dirs[:] = [...]), avoiding unnecessary filesystem traversal.

  4. When processing remote GitHub tree entries in crawl_github_files.py, path segments are evaluated against these patterns to avoid fetching entire Git tree hierarchies via REST.

  5. File Extension and Basename Patterns (*.ext, .filename):

  6. Extension-based patterns (*.pyc, *.lock, *.png) evaluate against the file's basename via fnmatch.fnmatch(filename, pattern).
  7. Fixed-name patterns (.DS_Store, package-lock.json, .env) require an exact match against the basename.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Because utils/exclude_patterns.py is a declarative, constant-only module, it does not define custom exceptions or execute dynamic logic that could raise runtime errors during initialization. However, its usage across the system involves specific defensive error-handling patterns:

  • Mutable State Isolation: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS is defined as a standard mutable Python set. If a consuming module were to mutate DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS directly (for example, by calling .add() or .clear()), those changes would alter exclusion behavior across the entire runtime process. Consuming crawlers in crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py treat this set as read-only by copying it (e.g., set(DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS)) or merging it with caller-specified patterns into a separate collection before traversing files.
  • Glob Evaluation Divergence: Standard Python fnmatch translates globs into regular expressions using re.escape internally. If a malformed pattern containing non-standard glob expressions is introduced, fnmatch.translate() can raise re.error. The current patterns rely strictly on standard wildcards (*, ?, []), ensuring valid regex compilation across all supported Python runtimes.
  • Path Separator Normalization: Standard fnmatch behavior on Windows can diverge when paths contain backslashes (\) instead of POSIX forward slashes (/). Consuming crawler modules defensively normalize paths to POSIX format using path.replace("\\", "/") prior to evaluating entries against DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS.

docs.title: files.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/files.py

Following the filtering and pattern sanitization established in exclude_patterns.py, the repository ingestion engine requires utilities to format, index, and retrieve source file contents efficiently. The utils/files.py module provides transformation and selective retrieval helpers that bridge raw ingested file tuples and downstream prompt synthesis nodes.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/files.py acts as a lightweight data transformation and selective access layer within the codebase documentation pipeline. After ingestion nodes (such as crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py) read source trees and filter out non-essential assets, the collected codebase is typically represented in memory as an ordered sequence of file paths and their contents. This module provides formatting tools to project this in-memory list into structural representations optimized for Large Language Model (LLM) prompts, as well as targeted accessors to pull specific file contents on demand.

The primary architectural role of files.py is optimizing LLM token budgets. Rather than injecting the entire codebase content into an initial reasoning prompt—which would rapidly exhaust context windows or incur excessive costs—the pipeline uses build_directory_tree() to construct a compact, human-readable directory hierarchy where each file is tagged with its zero-based integer index. Upstream analysis nodes (such as ContextRouter, IdentifyAbstractions, MapAbstractions, and CombineTutorial in nodes.py) provide this structural map to LLMs so they can evaluate project architecture and return lists of relevant file indices. Subsequently, get_content_for_indices() resolves those indices back into concrete file contents, loading only the source code necessary for detailed analysis.

docs.title: build_directory_tree()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_directory_tree(files_data: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> str:

Description: Constructs a compact, hierarchical directory tree formatted as a single string from an enumerated list of (path, content) tuples. Files are grouped by their parent directory paths, with root-level files assigned to ".". Directories and filenames within each directory are sorted lexicographically to guarantee deterministic output across different operating systems and execution runs. Each file entry is annotated with its integer index in files_data (e.g., basename (idx:0)), allowing downstream LLM nodes to reference files by index rather than passing full filesystem paths.

Parameters: * files_data (list[tuple[str, str]]): Ordered collection of two-element tuples, where index 0 is the relative file path string and index 1 is the decoded text content of the file.

Returns: * str: A multiline string displaying directory paths terminated with / followed by two-space indented file entries with appended (idx:{i}) identifiers.

Raises: * This function raises no custom exceptions. If files_data is malformed (e.g., contains items that cannot be unpacked into two variables), a standard Python ValueError or TypeError will propagate.

docs.title: Phase 1: Directory Grouping and Index Tagging
docs.text:
dir_files = defaultdict(list)
    for i, (path, _content) in enumerate(files_data):
        dirname = os.path.dirname(path) or "."
        basename = os.path.basename(path)
        dir_files[dirname].append(f"{basename} (idx:{i})")
In this phase, the function iterates over files_data using enumerate to preserve the original integer index of each file. It decomposes each file path into its directory component (dirname) and filename component (basename) using os.path.dirname and os.path.basename. If os.path.dirname(path) returns an empty string (indicating a file situated at the root of the scanned repository), the directory defaults to ".". The formatted string f"{basename} (idx:{i})" is appended to a list in a collections.defaultdict(list), grouping all files under their respective parent directories.

docs.title: Phase 2: Hierarchical Sorting and Tree String Formatting
docs.text:
lines = []
    for dirname in sorted(dir_files.keys()):
        lines.append(f"{dirname}/")
        lines.extend(f"  {fname}" for fname in sorted(dir_files[dirname]))
    return "\n".join(lines)
In this phase, the collected directories are sorted alphabetically using sorted(dir_files.keys()). For each directory, a header line is appended with a trailing slash (f"{dirname}/"). The function then iterates over the sorted list of filenames belonging to that directory (sorted(dir_files[dirname])), indenting each entry by two spaces (" "). Finally, all lines are joined with newline characters ("\n"), producing a unified textual representation of the project hierarchy.

Example: 

# Extracted from utils/files.py:
def build_directory_tree(files_data):
    """Build a compact directory tree string from the list of (path, content) tuples.

    Groups files by directory and formats as a hierarchical tree with file indices.
    Used by ContextRouter, IdentifyAbstractions, MapAbstractions, and CombineTutorial
    to give LLMs structural context about the project layout.
    """
    dir_files = defaultdict(list)
    for i, (path, _content) in enumerate(files_data):
        dirname = os.path.dirname(path) or "."
        basename = os.path.basename(path)
        dir_files[dirname].append(f"{basename} (idx:{i})")

    lines = []
    for dirname in sorted(dir_files.keys()):
        lines.append(f"{dirname}/")
        lines.extend(f"  {fname}" for fname in sorted(dir_files[dirname]))
    return "\n".join(lines)

docs.title: get_content_for_indices()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def get_content_for_indices(files_data: list[tuple[str, str]], indices: list[int] | set[int] | collections.abc.Iterable[int]) -> dict[str, str]:

Description: Extracts the text content for a targeted collection of integer indices from the files_data list. It performs bounds checking against the total length of files_data to silently ignore invalid or negative indices. For each valid index, it extracts the file path and content, assembling a dictionary whose key combines the integer index and the file path (formatted as "{i} # {path}"), with the value containing the raw file content string.

Parameters: * files_data (list[tuple[str, str]]): Ordered list of (path, content) tuples representing the ingested repository. * indices (Iterable[int]): An iterable collection of integer indices specifying which files should be extracted from files_data.

Returns: * dict[str, str]: A dictionary mapping formatted identifier strings ("{index} # {relative_path}") to their corresponding file content strings.

Raises: * This function raises no exceptions. Out-of-bounds indices are discarded via an explicit boundary condition check.

docs.title: Bounds Validation and Map Assembly
docs.text:
def get_content_for_indices(files_data, indices):
    """Get file content for specific indices from files_data list."""
    content_map = {}
    for i in indices:
        if 0 <= i < len(files_data):
            path, content = files_data[i]
            content_map[f"{i} # {path}"] = content  # Use index + path as key for context
    return content_map
The implementation initializes an empty content_map dictionary and iterates across each index i provided in indices. The conditional expression if 0 <= i < len(files_data) protects against negative indexing and IndexError exceptions caused by hallucinated or stale indices emitted by an LLM. When an index satisfies the bounds check, the function unpacks (path, content) from files_data[i] and stores the entry using the composite key f"{i} # {path}". This composite key ensures that downstream prompts retain both the numerical identifier and the human-readable path alongside the source code content.

Example: 

# Extracted from utils/files.py:
def get_content_for_indices(files_data, indices):
    """Get file content for specific indices from files_data list."""
    content_map = {}
    for i in indices:
        if 0 <= i < len(files_data):
            path, content = files_data[i]
            content_map[f"{i} # {path}"] = content  # Use index + path as key for context
    return content_map

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
utils/files.py relies on defensive programming patterns to ensure stability when processing variable inputs:

  • Index Bounds Protection: In get_content_for_indices(), caller-provided indices often originate from unvalidated LLM output strings that are parsed into integers. To prevent out-of-range indexing crashes, the function guards list access with if 0 <= i < len(files_data). Any index that is negative or greater than or equal to len(files_data) is bypassed without raising IndexError.
  • Root Directory Normalization: In build_directory_tree(), calling os.path.dirname(path) on a file located in the root directory (e.g., "main.py") yields an empty string "". The expression os.path.dirname(path) or "." intercepts this empty string and substitutes ".", ensuring that root-level files are grouped together under a valid directory entry.
  • Empty Collection Handling: If an empty list [] is passed to build_directory_tree(), the loop over files_data does not execute, dir_files remains empty, and the function cleanly returns an empty string "". Similarly, passing an empty index list or an empty files_data list to get_content_for_indices() cleanly returns an empty dictionary {}.

docs.title: mkdocs.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/mkdocs.py

Following the structural repository traversal and selective content retrieval orchestrated by files.py, the pipeline synthesizes generated documentation artifacts into publication-ready static sites. The utils/mkdocs.py module serves as the final rendering and serialization engine for the documentation pipeline, consolidating site configuration, recursive navigation grouping, index page synthesis, client-side diagram orchestration, and cross-chapter hyperlink normalization.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils/mkdocs.py module decouples documentation generation from specific output formats by managing the disk serialization and layout formatting for both MkDocs Material static sites and standalone Markdown bundles. Originally refactored from scattered static routines across nodes.py and utils/prompts.py, this component standardizes the creation of the mkdocs.yml specification, handles deep hierarchical navigation trees, and generates automated index matrices.

The module provides two distinct output pathways: 1. MkDocs Material Pipeline (write_mkdocs_output): Configures a complete documentation site featuring dark/light palettes, search plugins, interactive Panzoom pan/zoom controls, custom Mermaid diagram DOM un-wrapping, automated redirect landing pages (docs/index.md), rich API index matrices (docs/api/index.md), and deterministic relative link normalization. 2. Standalone Markdown Pipeline (write_standalone_output): Assembles decoupled Markdown files alongside an aggregated single-file document (full_content.md) complete with anchor-based tables of contents for portability.

For complex API reference documentation exceeding five modules, the module dynamically interfaces with call_llm.py to synthesize logical module groupings using domain reasoning, while falling back to structural filesystem hierarchies or flat navigation lists if inference fails or thresholds are unmet.

docs.title: build_mkdocs_config()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_mkdocs_config(site_name: str, nav_yaml: str, include_home: bool = True, lang_code: str = "") -> str:

Description: Programmatically constructs the text content of a complete mkdocs.yml configuration targeting the mkdocs-material theme. It configures code block copy buttons, search indexing, deep navigation indexes, light/slate dark mode toggles, and syntax highlighting via pymdownx.highlight and pymdownx.inlinehilite. To prevent Material's internal styling from clashing with custom Mermaid rendering, it binds Mermaid code blocks to the .mermaid-raw CSS class via pymdownx.superfences custom fences and configures the panzoom plugin to target .mermaid-raw selectors.

Parameters: * site_name (str): Title of the documentation site displayed in the MkDocs header and metadata. * nav_yaml (str): Raw navigation YAML string (typically generated by build_grouped_nav or provided in prep_res). * include_home (bool, optional): Whether to inject a - Home: index.md navigation entry. Defaults to True. * lang_code (str, optional): Two-letter ISO language code (e.g., "vi", "zh", "ja") for UI localization. Defaults to "".

Returns: * str: Fully formatted, ready-to-write mkdocs.yml configuration string.

Raises: * This function does not raise internal exceptions; string interpolation operations are fully deterministic.

Example: 

def build_mkdocs_config(site_name: str, nav_yaml: str, include_home: bool = True, lang_code: str = "") -> str:
    # Extract nav items from nav_snippet (strip the "nav:" header line)
    nav_lines = nav_yaml.split("\n")
    nav_body = "\n".join(nav_lines[1:]) if nav_lines else ""

    # Conditional Home nav entry (CI has root index.md, local mkdocs doesn't)
    home_line = "  - Home: index.md\n" if include_home else ""

    # Optional Material theme language (e.g. "vi", "zh", "ja", "ko")
    lang_line = f"  language: {lang_code}\n" if lang_code else ""

    return (
        f"site_name: '{site_name}'\n"
        f"theme:\n"
        f"  name: material\n"
        f"{lang_line}"
        f"  features:\n"
        f"    - content.code.copy\n"
        f"    - navigation.indexes\n"
        f"  palette:\n"
        f"    - scheme: default\n"
        f"      toggle:\n"
        f"        icon: material/brightness-7\n"
        f"        name: Switch to dark mode\n"
        f"    - scheme: slate\n"
        f"      toggle:\n"
        f"        icon: material/brightness-4\n"
        f"        name: Switch to light mode\n"
        f"plugins:\n"
        f"  - search\n"
        f"  - panzoom:\n"
        f"      include_selectors:\n"
        f"        - '.mermaid-raw'\n"
        f"markdown_extensions:\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.highlight:\n"
        f"      anchor_linenums: true\n"
        f"      use_pygments: true\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.superfences:\n"
        f"      custom_fences:\n"
        f"        - name: mermaid\n"
        f"          class: mermaid-raw\n"
        f"          format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.inlinehilite\n"
        f"extra_javascript:\n"
        f"  - https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@11/dist/mermaid.min.js\n"
        f"  - javascripts/mermaid-init.js\n"
        f"nav:\n"
        f"{home_line}"
        f"{nav_body}\n"
    )

The function handles string decomposition by splitting the input nav_yaml across newline boundaries and stripping the initial top-level nav: declaration, allowing the navigation tree to be nested cleanly under the root configuration. It selectively injects language attributes and home entry directives based on incoming flags, ensuring that local executions and continuous integration environments configure their respective landing hierarchies correctly. The returned YAML payload integrates CDN-hosted Mermaid runtime assets alongside local initialization hooks to ensure that diagrams render reliably upon DOM load.

docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_mermaid_init_js() -> str:

Description: Accessor function returning the embedded JavaScript script string (MERMAID_INIT_JS) required to bridge MkDocs Material, PyMdown Extensions, and Mermaid.js.

Parameters: * None.

Returns: * str: The complete client-side JavaScript source code string.

Raises: * No exceptions are raised.

Example: 

def build_mermaid_init_js() -> str:
    """Return the JavaScript snippet that initializes Mermaid diagrams."""
    return MERMAID_INIT_JS

The underlying script resolves a specific markup incompatibility between PyMdown SuperFences and Mermaid v11. Because SuperFences outputs <pre class="mermaid-raw"><code>...</code></pre>, the initialization script queries all matching preformatted tags, extracts the inner text from the nested <code> element, hoists that content directly into the <pre> container, and purges the child element before triggering mermaid.run(). This unwrapping prevents Mermaid syntax evaluation errors while maintaining strict diagram styling isolation from MkDocs CSS overrides.

docs.title: build_grouped_nav()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_grouped_nav(sections: list, chapter_files: list, indent: int = 4) -> list[str]:

Description: Recursively constructs formatted YAML navigation lines from an arbitrary-depth section grouping tree (derived from LLM clustering). For each section, it evaluates nested sub-sections under the children key and matches module leaf nodes against the chapter_files collection via module_name. It groups files within each section by their originating subdirectory (original_path), nesting non-root files within directory-specific sub-layers while keeping repository root files flat.

Parameters: * sections (list): A list of dictionaries representing logical sections, optionally containing nested children and modules lists. * chapter_files (list): List of chapter dictionaries containing metadata (module_name, filename, original_path). * indent (int, optional): Number of leading indentation spaces to apply to generated YAML lines. Defaults to 4.

Returns: * list[str]: An ordered collection of indented YAML lines representing the navigation tree.

Raises: * No explicit exceptions raised; missing module references in chapter_files are safely skipped via fallback iterators.

Example: 

def build_grouped_nav(sections: list, chapter_files: list, indent: int = 4) -> list[str]:
    emit_raw("DEBUG", f"build_grouped_nav | building nav for {len(sections)} sections", dest="LOG")
    from collections import defaultdict

    lines = []
    pad = " " * indent
    for section in sections:
        lines.append(f"{pad}- {section['name']}:")
        if "children" in section:
            lines.extend(build_grouped_nav(section["children"], chapter_files, indent + 2))

        # Collect matched modules with directory info
        matched = []
        for mod_name in section.get("modules", []):
            match = next((cf for cf in chapter_files if cf["module_name"] == mod_name), None)
            if match:
                dir_path = os.path.dirname(match.get("original_path", "")) or ""
                matched.append((dir_path, mod_name, match))

        # Group by directory
        dir_groups = defaultdict(list)
        for dir_path, mod_name, match in matched:
            dir_groups[dir_path].append((mod_name, match))

        # Emit dir sub-layers for non-root dirs, flat for root files
        has_non_root = any(d for d in dir_groups)
        if has_non_root:
            for dir_path in sorted(dir_groups.keys()):
                if dir_path:
                    # Non-root: add directory sub-layer with bare module names
                    lines.append(f"{pad}  - {dir_path}:")
                    for mod_name, match in dir_groups[dir_path]:
                        lines.append(f"{pad}    - '{mod_name}': 'api/{match['filename']}'")
                else:
                    # Root files: flat (no sub-layer)
                    for mod_name, match in dir_groups[dir_path]:
                        lines.append(f"{pad}  - '{mod_name}': 'api/{match['filename']}'")
        else:
            # All root files → flat list
            for _dir_path, mod_name, match in matched:
                lines.append(f"{pad}  - '{mod_name}': 'api/{match['filename']}'")

    return lines

The algorithm navigates the grouping tree by applying indentation proportional to the recursion depth (indent + 2 for nested sub-sections). To avoid chaotic menu layouts when many files share a logical category, it extracts the parent directory path via os.path.dirname on each file's original_path. By organizing items through a defaultdict(list), the method injects intermediate structural folders only when non-root files are present, emitting bare module names scoped cleanly within their parent folder paths.

docs.title: collect_all_modules()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def collect_all_modules(sections: list) -> set:

Description: Recursively traverses a hierarchical section dictionary tree to extract and aggregate all referenced module_name strings into a unified set. Used primarily for post-grouping validation to identify orphaned modules dropped during LLM synthesis.

Parameters: * sections (list): List of section dictionaries that may contain modules (list of strings) and children (nested section lists).

Returns: * set: Unordered set containing every string module name present across the entire hierarchy.

Raises: * No exceptions raised.

Example: 

def collect_all_modules(sections: list) -> set:
    """Recursively collect all module names referenced in a sections tree."""
    result = set()
    for section in sections:
        result.update(section.get("modules", []))
        if "children" in section:
            result.update(collect_all_modules(section["children"]))
    return result

This helper implements a classic tree traversal pattern, accumulating module identifiers at each level using set.update() before descending into any nested structures within section["children"]. The resulting collection provides a complete list of all clustered modules, enabling callers to run set-difference operations against original input files to detect omissions.

docs.title: write_mkdocs_output()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def write_mkdocs_output(output_path, prep_res, chapter_files):

Description: Main orchestrator for generating static MkDocs documentation. It resolves navigation hierarchies (leveraging LLM clustering when appropriate), writes configuration files, builds landing and redirect pages, executes deterministic cross-chapter link normalization, and serializes final Markdown chapters to disk.

Parameters: * output_path (str): Base output directory where the documentation hierarchy and mkdocs.yml will be created. * prep_res (dict): Pipeline metadata dictionary containing project configuration, navigation snippets, mode settings, translation keys, and prompt inputs. * chapter_files (list[dict]): Ordered list of generated chapter payloads, including filenames, module names, summaries, and Markdown text.

Returns: * None

Raises: * OSError / IOError: Raised if the target filesystem directories cannot be created or file write operations fail.

docs.title: Phase 1: Output Directory Initialization & Mode Setup
docs.text:
The function initializes directory structures, creates docs/api, and sets localized site branding based on pipeline operational modes:

    project_name = prep_res["project_name"]
    mode = prep_res["mode"]
    api_docs_path = os.path.join(output_path, "docs", "api")
    os.makedirs(api_docs_path, exist_ok=True)

    mode_labels = {
        "tutorial": get("UI_MODE_TUTORIAL"),
        "advanced": get("UI_MODE_ADVANCED"),
        "sdk": get("UI_MODE_SDK"),
        "api-reference": get("UI_MODE_API_REF"),
    }

    emit("COMBINE_FORMAT_MKDOCS", mode=mode_labels.get(mode, "Documentation"))
